note: Golden vectors of the loop law (CONTRACT §5a). Every implementation of the law runs every case. A case: `spec` planned against `ctx` gives `plan`; an implementation that only steps starts from `plan`. Then tick by tick: `set` ({params, ramp_ms?}), when present, changes params ahead of the tick; `inputs` are the readings by signal name (null = no value); `dt` is the time since the previous tick in ms. `expect.outputs` has one value per output of the plan, in its order. `expect.signals` has, per signal, its value, integral and derivative after the tick (all 0 while the loop settles). Numbers are equal within 1e-9. `guard` and `end` are present exactly on the tick that ends the loop. Where the numbers come from: `expect.outputs`, `guard` and `end` of a case without a `note` were worked out by hand. `plan`, `expect.signals`, and the outputs of the cases with a `note` were written by packages/protocol/loop.ts. Porting to Python 3.5: the order of a tick's inputs is the order of `plan.signals`, an array, and never the key order of `spec.signals` or of `inputs` (a dict has no order there; load with object_pairs_hook=OrderedDict if an order is needed). A reading is a number only when it is an int or a float and not a bool (bool is a subclass of int), finite, and within ±1e9; anything else is no value. Use true division and floats throughout, compare with the same strict and non-strict signs as loop.ts, and keep each expression's order of operations: a × b / c is (a × b) / c.
